answer.label: Really Toni Morrison — but the popular wording is lightly reworded
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Toni Morrison remark, made in a 1981 speech to the Ohio Arts Council and reported in The Cincinnati Enquirer. But her documented words were “If you find a book you really want to read but it hasn’t been written yet, then you must write it” — the viral form (“If there’s a book that you want to read…”) is a lightly smoothed paraphrase, not a verbatim quotation.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: “Writing Is Third Career For Morrison” (The Cincinnati Enquirer)

source.excerpt: If you find a book you really want to read but it hasn’t been written yet, then you must write it.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the line to Morrison’s 1981 Ohio Arts Council speech and credits her for the remark.

The earliest documented print is “Writing Is Third Career For Morrison” by Ellen Brown, The Cincinnati Enquirer, 27 Sep 1981 (per QI’s citation), where her words were “If you find a book you really want to read…”.
The smoothed “If there’s a book that you want to read…” form now circulates on Goodreads and countless writing sites.
source.excerptNote: Morrison’s documented 1981 words, as reported by Ellen Brown in The Cincinnati Enquirer. The popular internet version (“If there’s a book that you want to read…”) is a lightly smoothed rewording of this.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: the full investigation and 1981 citation

source.rightsNote: Morrison’s remark was first published in 1981 (The Cincinnati Enquirer), well after the 1931 US public-domain cutoff, so her words remain in copyright. Rights to Morrison’s expression rest with her estate; the newspaper report itself is held by its publisher (Gannett).

author.name: Toni Morrison
author.heading: About Toni Morrison
author.metaLine: 1931–2019 · American novelist, editor, and Nobel laureate
author.bio: Toni Morrison (born Chloe Ardelia Wofford in Lorain, Ohio) was one of the most celebrated American novelists of the twentieth century, author of The Bluest Eye, Song of Solomon, and Beloved. She won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1988 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993. Before her career as a novelist she worked as an influential editor at Random House — the “third career” framing of the 1981 newspaper piece that first reported this remark.

misattribution.heading: Right author, reworded line
misattribution.intro: This one is not a misattribution — the sentiment and the remark are genuinely Toni Morrison’s. The catch is the wording: the version everyone shares has been quietly smoothed from what she actually said, and a few antecedent thinkers had voiced the same idea long before 1981.

items.who: “If there’s a book that you want to read…” vs. what she said
items.why: Morrison’s documented 1981 words were “If you find a book you really want to read but it hasn’t been written yet, then you must write it.” The viral form drops “find” and “really” and inserts “that” — a paraphrase, per Quote Investigator.
Disraeli reportedly quipped, “Madam, when I want to read a book, I write one” — a related sentiment, but not the same line, noted by QI.

items.who: C. S. Lewis (via J. R. R. Tolkien, 1955)
items.why: Tolkien credited Lewis with “if they won’t write the kind of books we want to read, we shall have to write them ourselves” — the same impulse, differently phrased (QI).

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the credit belongs to Toni Morrison, from her 1981 Ohio Arts Council speech — just quote her actual words, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it resonated
lead: Morrison made the remark not as a novelist but while still known as a senior editor at Random House — the 1981 newspaper piece framed writing as her “third career.” In context she described writing as “an advanced and slow form of reading,” which is what gives the line its punch: the writer is first a hungry reader who refuses to wait.

The thought struck a nerve with aspiring authors and became one of the most-shared pieces of writing advice on the internet — which is exactly how the wording drifted into its smoother, more quotable modern shape.
